visuals.title: Complications
visuals.text: Lungs: infection, pneumothorax, respiratory failure. Heart: cor pulmonale, RV hypertrophy. Blood: polycythaemia.

visual.caption: RV strain in V1 to V3. Also look for P pulmonale (tall inferior P waves) and right axis deviation.

visual.label: Example: FEV1 45%
visual.caption: All need FEV1/FVC below 0.7 after a bronchodilator.

facts.label: kPa plus oedema, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension

visual.label: Example 7.29, PaCO2 raised
visual.caption: Respiratory acidosis with a raised PaCO2 despite medical treatment.

glossary.Persistent airflow limitation: Narrowing of the airways that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator.
glossary.Occupational exposure: Breathing in dusts, fumes or chemicals at work, such as in mining or welding.
glossary.Dyspnoea on exertion: Breathlessness brought on by physical activity.
glossary.Sputum: Mucus coughed up from the lungs.
glossary.Purulent sputum: Yellow or green sputum containing pus, suggesting infection.
glossary.Prolonged expiratory phase: Breathing out taking longer than normal because air leaves narrowed airways slowly.
glossary.Wheeze: A whistling sound, mainly on breathing out, from narrowed airways.
glossary.Accessory muscle use: Using neck and shoulder muscles to help breathe, a sign of respiratory distress.
glossary.Acute exacerbation: A sudden worsening of COPD symptoms beyond usual day-to-day variation.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: measures pH, oxygen, carbon dioxide and bicarbonate in arterial blood.
glossary.HCO3-: Bicarbonate, the main buffer in blood; the kidneys retain it to correct an acidosis.
glossary.Hypoventilation: Breathing too little to clear carbon dioxide, so CO2 rises in the blood.
glossary.Renal compensation: The kidneys keeping more bicarbonate to bring a low pH back towards normal over days.
glossary.Respiratory acidosis: A low blood pH caused by CO2 building up from inadequate breathing.
glossary.Tension pneumothorax: Air trapped in the pleural space under pressure, pushing the heart across and stopping blood return: an emergency.
glossary.Hypoxia: Low oxygen levels in the tissues.
glossary.Right ventricular hypertrophy: Thickening of the right ventricle wall from pumping against high lung pressures.
glossary.Pulmonary function testing: Breathing tests including spirometry, lung volumes and gas transfer.
glossary.Hemi-diaphragm: The left or right half of the diaphragm as seen on a chest X-ray.
glossary.Hyperlucent: Appearing darker than normal on X-ray because there is more air and less tissue.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity.
glossary.Inferior leads: ECG leads II, III and aVF, which look at the bottom of the heart.
glossary.Low-voltage QRS: Small QRS complexes on the ECG, here because over-inflated lungs insulate the heart.
glossary.R/S transition: The chest lead where the R wave becomes bigger than the S wave, normally around V3 to V4.
glossary.RBBB: Right bundle branch block: delayed conduction in the right ventricle, giving a wide QRS with RSR' in V1.
glossary.Diurnal variation: Change in a measurement across the day, such as peak flow lower in the morning.
glossary.Eosinophil count: The number of eosinophils in the blood; raised levels suggest steroid-responsive disease.
glossary.Long-term oxygen therapy: Oxygen used at home for at least 15 hours a day to improve survival in chronic hypoxia.
glossary.Tiotropium: A long-acting antimuscarinic bronchodilator (LAMA) taken once daily.
glossary.Formoterol: A long-acting beta-2 agonist that also works quickly.
glossary.Pneumonia: Infection of the lung tissue; inhaled steroids increase the risk in COPD.
glossary.PaCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood; normal is about 4.7 to 6.0 kPa.
glossary.PaO2: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood; normal is about 10 to 13 kPa.
glossary.Upper lobe emphysema: Emphysema mainly in the top of the lungs, typical of smoking and suitable for volume reduction surgery.
glossary.Pneumococcal vaccine: A vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae, given once in COPD.
glossary.Prophylaxis: Treatment given to prevent a disease or episode rather than to treat it.
glossary.Prolonged QT: A long QT interval on ECG, which raises the risk of dangerous arrhythmias; macrolides can lengthen it.
glossary.Peripheral oedema: Swelling of the ankles and legs from fluid build-up.
glossary.Prednisolone: An oral corticosteroid, given for 5 days in an exacerbation.
glossary.Amoxicillin: A penicillin antibiotic, first-line for infective exacerbations.
glossary.Doxycycline: A tetracycline antibiotic, an option if allergic to penicillin.
glossary.Clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic, an option if allergic to penicillin.
glossary.Non-invasive ventilation: Breathing support through a tight-fitting face mask rather than a tube in the airway.
glossary.Macrophages: Immune cells that engulf debris and release inflammatory signals and proteases.
glossary.Proteases: Enzymes that break down proteins, including the elastin of lung tissue.
glossary.Antiprotease: A molecule that blocks protease enzymes and protects the lung from damage.
glossary.Alveolar septa: The thin walls between alveoli where gas exchange happens.
glossary.Gas trapping: Air left stuck in the lungs at the end of breathing out because airways close early.
glossary.Pulmonary vasoconstriction: Narrowing of the lung blood vessels, which raises pressure in the pulmonary arteries.
glossary.Vascular remodelling: Thickening of blood vessel walls over time, making the narrowing permanent.
glossary.Hypercapnia: A raised level of carbon dioxide in the blood.
glossary.Bicarbonate reabsorption: The kidneys taking bicarbonate back into the blood instead of excreting it.
